meta.title: Law, Rights & Kinship
meta.review: Professional legal and cultural review pending. No government or community endorsement claimed.
meta.lead: Understand rights. Respect kinship. Know where to ask.
meta.scope: Selected Australian and WA topics, with separately attributed cultural learning. This is not every law, personal legal advice or an automated legal decision.
meta.time: Sources checked 19 October 2026. This is a fixed review date, not a live law feed. Laws and commencement dates can change; check the official source and the law at the time of an event.
meta.privacy: Reading works offline. Source websites open only after a tap. This section does not upload reflections, determine guilt, certify consent or calculate cultural identity.
meta.framing: Living across legal and cultural systems in WA: many Aboriginal Nations have their own laws, kinship and responsibilities. Australian and WA legislation also applies; recognition and interaction depend on the particular law and context.

topics.title: Living across legal and cultural systems
topics.summary: People can live with Aboriginal laws, kinship and cultural responsibilities as well as Australian and WA legislation. These systems have different sources of authority and interact in particular ways.
can: Learn whose Country and community a cultural account concerns, and ask the appropriate knowledge holders how it applies.
Check whether a legal question involves federal, state or territory law, or a local rule.
limits: WA is home to many Aboriginal Nations and diverse communities. “Two societies” is too broad to describe everyone’s identity or legal position.
Cultural recognition does not create a general exemption from legislation. Recognition depends on the particular law, rights and circumstances.
topics.question: Which legal rule and which community’s cultural responsibility am I trying to understand?

topics.title: Marriage equality and who can marry
topics.summary: The right to marry does not depend on sex or gender. Two women, two men and couples including trans or non-binary people can marry when they meet the usual legal requirements.
can: Choose whether and whom to marry, with the other person’s free agreement.
Ask an authorised celebrant about identification, notice and the ceremony.
limits: Marriage involves two people, and neither can already be married. Prohibited family relationships also apply.
The usual marriage age is 18. A 16- or 17-year-old needs exceptional court approval and required consents to marry an adult; nobody under 16 can marry.
topics.question: What paperwork, notice and eligibility requirements apply to us?

topics.title: Three adults in a relationship
topics.jurisdiction: Australia · WA property and family-law questions need advice
topics.summary: Three consenting adults can choose a relationship together. Such a relationship is different from a legally recognised marriage involving all three people.
can: Discuss boundaries, commitments and each adult’s freedom to agree, disagree or leave.
Ask a WA family lawyer about property, wills, parenting and any de facto rights arising from your particular relationships.
limits: Current Australian law does not allow all three people to marry each other. A person already married cannot enter another legal marriage.
A throuple does not automatically receive all the rights of a married couple. Different laws may treat the individual relationships differently.
topics.question: What rights and obligations arise for each person, and what arrangements need individual advice?

topics.title: Consent is a continuing choice
topics.summary: Consent means freely agreeing to the particular sexual activity at the time. Anyone can change their mind, including after activity has started.
can: Say yes, no, pause or stop, and ask whether the other person freely wants to continue.
Stop when consent is withdrawn or is unclear; seek help if you feel pressured.
limits: A person who is asleep or unconscious cannot consent. Intoxication can prevent a person from freely consenting.
A signature, relationship, marriage, past agreement, affection or apparent enjoyment cannot replace current consent. An app cannot certify consent or prevent someone reporting harm.
topics.question: Is everyone freely choosing this now, with capacity and room to stop?

topics.title: Age, authority and sexual safety
topics.jurisdiction: Western Australia only · other jurisdictions differ
topics.summary: Legal Aid WA explains that the general age of sexual consent in WA is 16. A higher age of 18 applies to specified relationships involving care, supervision or authority.
can: Ask a qualified service about exact ages, roles and the applicable law.
Seek child-safety advice when a child may be at risk, even if some details are uncertain.
limits: A “yes” does not make conduct lawful where age, authority or prohibited-relative rules prevent it.
The age of sexual consent is different from marriage eligibility and rules about sexual images. This summary is not a defence, eligibility test or permission for conduct.
topics.question: What are the exact ages, relationship and positions of authority involved?

topics.title: Control, family violence and protection
topics.summary: Coercive control can involve a pattern of behaviours that restricts freedom. WA’s family-violence definition includes coercion, control, fear and the cumulative effect of behaviour.
can: Seek advice about safety planning, support and whether a restraining order may be available.
Record specific behaviours and their dates when doing so is safe.
limits: Not every hurt feeling, disagreement or unkind act is a criminal offence. The conduct, context and relevant law matter.
The family-violence definition is not itself proof of a standalone coercive-control offence. This card does not declare such an offence commenced or decide whether any offence occurred.
topics.question: What protection or advice is available while the facts and applicable offences are clarified?

topics.title: Marriage must be freely chosen
topics.summary: Forced marriage is a crime. Pressure can include threats, violence, deception or severe emotional pressure. It is not confined to any culture, religion or gender.
can: Decline a marriage and seek help if you cannot freely choose.
Have family involvement in introductions or arrangements while both people remain free to consent or refuse.
limits: Family, cultural or religious expectations cannot replace each person’s free and full consent.
An arranged marriage with free consent is different from a forced marriage. Offences can involve cultural or religious ceremonies as well as civil ones.
topics.question: Can each person safely refuse without coercion or punishment?

topics.title: Privacy, recording and keeping evidence
topics.jurisdiction: WA recording law · Australian digital-safety guidance
topics.summary: Keeping a dated account of what you observed can help you ask for advice. Secretly recording private conversations or activities, or sharing recordings, is restricted in WA.
can: Separate what you directly observed, what someone told you, interpretations and unknowns.
Ask about lawful, safe evidence collection and keep original digital context when appropriate.
limits: Being part of a conversation does not automatically make every secret recording or disclosure lawful. Exceptions need legal advice.
Do not put yourself at risk to collect evidence. Recording law in another state may differ; public accusations may also create legal risks.
topics.question: What can I lawfully preserve or share, and could collecting it increase danger?

topics.title: Intimate images and online safety
topics.summary: Sharing or threatening to share someone’s intimate image without consent can be unlawful. Consent to one use does not automatically authorise other uses.
can: Ask for help with image-based abuse and use the official reporting and removal pathways.
Respect each person’s separate choice about taking, keeping and sharing intimate material.
limits: Rules concerning sexual images of people under 18 are different from the age of sexual consent. Do not create, request or circulate those images; seek qualified advice about handling existing material.
Specific legal definitions and exceptions matter. This app does not authorise sharing or ask you to upload intimate images.
topics.question: What reporting or removal option applies, and how should existing material be handled safely?

topics.title: Child safety and reporting concerns
topics.summary: You can ask WA Child Protection for advice about a child’s safety or wellbeing. A concern can be raised without an app establishing that abuse occurred.
can: Describe direct observations, who said what, dates, missing details and any immediate risk.
Ask an appropriate service about next steps and any reporting duties attached to your profession or role.
limits: A report is not a finding of guilt. Do not repeatedly question a child or attempt your own investigation.
Reporting duties depend on the role, facts and current legislation. In immediate danger in Australia, call 000.
topics.question: What needs protection now, and what firsthand information does the service need?

topics.title: Equality and discrimination complaints
topics.jurisdiction: Australia-wide federal protections · state pathways also exist
topics.summary: Federal discrimination laws protect people on specified grounds in areas of public life. These include race, disability, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and other grounds.
can: Ask about a discrimination complaint involving work, education, housing or services.
Keep a factual account and seek advice about the right complaint body and relevant time limits.
limits: Coverage and exceptions depend on the law and circumstances. Not every disagreement or unfair experience meets a legal definition.
Marriage equality does not mean every other law or service rule is identical across states and territories.
topics.question: Which protected ground, public activity and complaint pathway may apply?

topics.title: Noongar kinship, family and responsibilities
topics.jurisdiction: Selected public Whadjuk / Nyungar accounts · south-west WA
topics.summary: Derbal Nara’s public Nyungar accounts connect family, Country and knowledge. Its Whadjuk account describes inherited social groups, relationships and responsibilities to care for totems.
can: Follow the named public accounts and ask relevant family or community knowledge holders for guidance.
Use the existing Living connections section to explore other separately attributed accounts.
limits: This Whadjuk account is not a universal rule for all Noongar families, Yamatji peoples or other Aboriginal Nations.
The app does not assign anyone a skin group, totem, cultural authority or permitted partner. Cultural review remains pending.
topics.question: Whose account is this, and who has authority to explain its application to my family?

topics.title: Cultural kinship and legal family categories
topics.summary: Kinship includes relationships and responsibilities that may extend beyond a simple biological family tree. A cultural family term alone does not establish a particular legal relationship.
can: Explain the meaning of family terms and the actual relationship when speaking with a service or lawyer.
Ask the relevant community about kinship, and a qualified lawyer about the particular legal rule.
limits: Do not assume that a cultural term such as brother, sister, aunty or uncle proves a particular biological or legal relationship.
Legal prohibitions involving relatives, age or authority still need examination. The app cannot determine ancestry, partner eligibility or whether conduct is lawful from a name or family label.
topics.question: What does this kinship term mean here, and what relationship does the relevant law actually define?

topics.title: How Australian law can recognise cultural rights
topics.jurisdiction: Australia-wide framework · rights specific to group and Country
topics.summary: Native title is one example of Australian law recognising rights and interests connected with traditional laws and customs. Applications and determinations concern particular groups, land and waters.
can: Read the relevant public determination and seek guidance from the proper Traditional Owner body or legal service.
Keep cultural authority, native title rights and a particular statutory obligation clearly identified.
limits: Native title is not a general permission to enter every place or exercise any claimed right. The actual determination and other laws matter.
It does not create a general exemption from criminal law or decide family, marriage or consent questions. This app does not determine native title.
topics.question: Which group, area, determination and legal question are involved?

topics.title: Children: safety, family and cultural connection
topics.jurisdiction: Western Australia · parenting and child-protection contexts differ
topics.summary: Legal Aid WA explains that parenting decisions for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children consider their right to enjoy culture and connections with family, community, Country and language.
can: Ask how the child’s safety, views and cultural connections will be considered together.
Ask about Aboriginal family-led decision-making or an appropriate Aboriginal service, including local eligibility.
limits: Cultural connection does not remove child-safety duties, and family wishes do not automatically decide a parenting order.
The Aboriginal Family Led Decision Making program operates in specified locations and circumstances; it is not a guaranteed option everywhere.
topics.question: Who can support this child’s safety and cultural connections in the process involved?

topics.title: Who can share cultural knowledge?
topics.jurisdiction: Relevant Aboriginal Nation, community and knowledge holders
topics.summary: The AIATSIS ethics framework centres Indigenous self-determination, leadership, consent and accountability. Community knowledge holders guide whether and how particular knowledge can be shared.
can: Use clearly attributed public material within its stated scope and permissions.
Ask appropriate knowledge holders about restricted material, consent, attribution and review.
limits: A public web page is not permission to copy everything, reveal restricted knowledge or speak for a whole community.
This app claims no community endorsement. It does not publish restricted teachings, adjudicate cultural disputes or present ethical guidance as a new criminal law.
topics.question: Who has authority to give permission, and what conditions apply to this specific use?

topics.title: How a proposal becomes law
topics.jurisdiction: Federal Parliament · WA has its own law-making process
topics.status: Parliamentary process; proposals are not current law
topics.summary: A wish, petition, recommendation or bill is different from a law that is in force. For federal legislation, both houses must agree on the bill and it receives Royal Assent; commencement also matters.
can: Identify which Parliament has responsibility, read the bill and check the official status and start date.
Use evidence and community perspectives to explain the change you want.
limits: Marriage law is federal. WA alone cannot create a recognised three-person marriage under the current federal framework.
A meeting with an official, a grant or an app feature does not mean Parliament has approved the project or changed a law.
topics.question: Is this an idea, consultation, bill, enacted law or provision that has actually commenced?

topics.title: Have your say in Parliament
topics.jurisdiction: Choose federal or WA process for the issue
topics.summary: People can raise proposals with their representatives, use parliamentary petitions and contribute to relevant committee inquiries. The rules depend on the Parliament, House and inquiry.
can: For federal matters, read the House of Representatives petition rules or a relevant committee’s submission instructions.
For WA matters, follow the WA Parliament’s petition guidance and seek the appropriate member or committee.
limits: A petition does not guarantee a law change. A submission may become public; check confidentiality arrangements before including personal or cultural information.
The app does not send your writing, sign a petition, lodge a submission or speak for a community.
topics.question: What change am I requesting, which body can act, and what evidence can I lawfully and respectfully share?
